headline: Brazil's emergency alert system hacked with 'misanthropy' message
summary: Hackers are suspected of sending an unauthorized "extreme" alert to cell phones across Brazil, displaying a message of 'misanthropy' and causing authorities to take the system offline.
details: An unauthorized alert message, reading "misantropi4" (a leetspeak version of "misanthropy"), was sent to cell phones in several Brazilian states on Saturday morning. The Brazilian government suspects a hacker attack was responsible for the incident.

The alert, categorized as "extreme," was first received in the southern state of Paraná, followed by warnings in major cities like São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. This emergency text system is similar to the US's Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA).

Following the incident, Brazil's National Civil Defense took its warning platform offline, citing a likely hacker attack. Authorities are working to restore the tool once security conditions are reestablished.

The National Civil Defense stated that the false alert was remotely triggered by an unauthorized individual, not an official of the National Civil Protection and Defense System. The message's content, "hatred towards humanity," strongly suggests a malicious intent.

Civil Defense agencies in São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro confirmed that the alert was not issued by their agents and that no real-world incident justified such a warning. The Cellbroadcast tool used for these alerts has been temporarily disabled.

Investigations into the origin of the message are underway, involving Anatel (National Telecommunications Agency) and other relevant institutions. Residents in affected areas also reported receiving the alert via SMS in addition to the Cellbroadcast platform.

headline_marked: [[SMPTE Makes All Standards Freely Accessible]] to boost innovation
headline: SMPTE Makes All Standards Freely Accessible to boost innovation
summary: The Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers is removing all access barriers to its extensive catalog of standards, aiming to accelerate adoption and drive future innovation in media technology.
details: SMPTE, the global professional organization for media technologists, has announced that its entire catalog of Standards, Recommended Practices, Engineering Guidelines, and Registered Disclosure Documents (RDDs) is now available free of charge. This move, effective immediately, includes all future releases.

For over a century, SMPTE Standards have been crucial for ensuring interoperability within the entertainment technology industry. By making these resources freely accessible, SMPTE aims to lower adoption barriers, foster greater implementation, and stimulate the next wave of innovation.

SMPTE President Rich Welsh stated that the decision was made to address transformative shifts in the industry, such as IP-based workflows and AI authenticity. He emphasized that opening access ensures a stronger, more accessible foundation for future media technology.

This initiative is part of SMPTE's broader effort to modernize its Standards development and publication processes. The organization has adopted GitHub-based workflows, transitioned to structured HTML authoring, and implemented an integrated publishing pipeline for streamlined document management.

Raymond Yeung, SMPTE Standards Vice President, highlighted that open access enhances transparency and allows SMPTE to respond more rapidly to industry needs while maintaining the quality of its Standards.

This transition is supported by SMPTE's Diamond-level Corporate Members, including Amazon AWS, Apple, Blackmagic Design, CBS/Paramount Global, Disney, Dolby, Fox, Google, Ross Video, Sony, and Telstra. Companies and individuals pledging significant donations will be recognized as Inaugural Supporters.

SMPTE Standards Director Steve LLamb noted that standards are most valuable when universally accessible, leading to more consistent implementation and reduced misinformation. This open approach supports developers, integrators, educators, manufacturers, and emerging markets.
